annotations.text:
D · the expanding band

The scoreboard is an instrument, not a control, so it wears no key box and sits nowhere near MENU. Shut, it is a bare readout at top center, each side a two-line stack in its color: in Melee the team's name over its score, in the duel the pilot's call sign over their rating, with no score and no rung line, since neither says anything a duel's readout doesn't say better. The expand affordance is the instrument grammar's own: the faint corner brackets the radar wears, brightened while open. Pressed, the readout grows out of the band, so shut and open are one object at two depths. PLAYERS is gone; the readout carries the roster.

The open panel is the shipped players panel's grammar: section heads in dim capitals with their column labels on the line, dashed rules between sections. Sections are the modularity. Every zone stacks one pilot list, the sides told apart by the color the names already wear, with no team heads, since the band above carries the names and scores. The duel adds its run of fights; a pressed row opens the same pilot card in every zone.

Desktop shows Melee open. Portrait shows the duel open with a pressed row's card. Landscape shows the band shut.

Held constant: the shipped chrome (hamburger MENU, LINK, the radar) and the fight behind the glass. Desktop shows Melee mid-match, Pylon 15 to Caisson 19; landscape shows the ladder at the moment a rung clears, where the giant mid-screen banner lives today; portrait shows the ladder mid-life, the shape that overruns today.

Events land beside the chassis in the scoring side's color for a few seconds instead of as 24pt white across the middle. DESTROYED and SUDDEN DEATH are the same kind of tenant.

A · the scorebug

One contained box top center, broadcast style: side chips, scores, clock, and the zone's slot on its foot. The box has a hard cap, so portrait cannot overrun; its type rides the window, so a desktop reads it across the room. Cost: it is furniture over the fight's top edge, and on short windows it crowds the glass.

B · the corner tile

The scoreboard as an instrument, docked under MENU where chrome already lives. Clock at the head, a row per side, the zone line at the foot; an event appends a colored row that fades. The center of the glass stays empty, which portrait loves. Cost: the score stops being the first thing a stranger sees, and anyone raised on broadcast sport expects it centered.

C · the edge strip

The window's top edge is the scoreboard: a slim bar filled from each end in the sides' colors, in proportion, numbers at the ends, clock dead center. The zone line hangs in a tab under the clock; an event flashes the bar in the scoring side's color and prints in the tab. Adapts to any width by construction. Cost: the fill says the score a second way, it jumps rather than creeps in a legs game like Ladder, and the strip's own height caps how big the numbers can get.

The first three directions, kept for the record. Chris picked D, on the Clock key page. All four share the chassis idea: score and clock common to every zone, a zone-owned place for what the zone knows, events in the scoring side's color instead of the mid-screen banner.
